Reviewed on February 15, 2016. Not a blocker for 11. Might be worth testing to verify. Requires a particular user interface configuration, more of an edge case and doesn't seem like a big impact to the student.

As soon as this is approved by the moderator though the student is able to view it. I consider this a lower level issue because it seems like the biggest thing it's blocking them from seeing is the comments on a denied post.

This is still an issue and affects versions going forward, including 22x.

I don't think this should be set to minor because if the student's post gets denied, they have no clue that it has been denied. In this case, the instructor, (if they are even aware that the student can't view their own post and the comment cannot be viewed by the student), would have to email any students when denying their posts.

Since the student is unable to view their own post in this case the student has no idea of the state of their post and would still be waiting on the instructor.
I still feel this is good for QAReview and is more of an expected functionality and/or best practice.

If the student with the denied post makes another post and it gets approved, only then do they get to see their previous (denied) post with the instructor's comment.

I think not being able to see their own pending post is a big issue. As a student, I would be annoyed if I made a long post and then it doesn't display and would assume it "disappeared" and would probably repost (which wouldn't show either).

Wilma reached out to me last week to ask whether the collapsible sections issue in Lessons has been resolved, as it is one of the outstanding items that they have on their list for  the Sakai Technical Roadmap. I went ahead and retested this on Sakai 25 (Maria DB branch) using JAWS+Chrome) following the test steps on the Jira ticket, and it seems to be working for me, except for two minor glitches that I’m noticing.



1--When I navigate to the Lessons page, and the collapsible section is set to its collapsed state, the placeholder/helper text does say, “click to expand”, but its also announcing the current state of the control as “expanded” even though the section is collapsed.



2--If you press enter to “expand” the collapsed section, it will changed to its expanded state, but there is no dynamic announcement that this has happened - you can only tell once you tab down into the main content of the Lessons page where the section will have been expanded.



I created a short demo video (see attached) to document these issues.



Again, as a screen reader user, I have no way of replicating/verifying the issues that Alan is saying that he is experiencing while using just the keyboard with Chrome, but we do occasionally run into situations like this where something will work for screen reader users, but won’t work when just using the keyboard (without having a screen reader enabled) and I’m not sure why??

In the meantime, can someone please confirm whether the "Expand All" and "Collapse All" button at the top is keyboard accessible? I was able to "tab" through the interface and expand all/collapse all with my keyboard so on the surface it seems so.  I want to be sure this is confirmed and users can access content through this process until individual sections can be made accessible.

As an instructor, I like the collapsible section option for some content to make it more "app-like" and to declutter the page. Even though I don't have any students that use assistive technologies right now, I want to be sure that my design choices can help all learners, whether if someone's situation changes during the current semester (e.g. accident or illness) or students in future classes who may use assistive tools.

I did this on purpose. If you choose to grade an assignment and you pick points, it goes to the gradebook. Eventually, the assignment tool won’t store point scores at all, they will all be in the grading service.

However, I thought it might be a bit contentious\! My reasoning here, and this is around the centralised grading concept, is that if a tool grades something, like, you check a box to grade something, then the grading service and the gradebook is where it should go. We have way too much overlap in grading functionality across tools and it increased our maintenance burden.
Added the TL label. This is such a drastic change from previous behavior, I think the TL group needs to weigh in.
I totally agree.
Can we please have our checkbox back?

We can have the checkbox back. However … what that implies is that we will always have duplicate grading structures in assignments, so the score db column, the feedback attachments, the private notes, all that stuff that’s in assignments that should really be in the grading service where all tools can use it. The centralised grading service work is all about enriching the grading service and removing grading logic from the tools wherever possible, thus simplifying our code base while actually making it more powerful. So, I’d like T&L to discuss this - I’ll come to the call and make the case.
Currently quizzes are not required to be sent to the GB. Whatever is decided, I think it should be consistent between assignments and T&Q.

An additional consideration/point against removing the “Send grades to Gradebook” checkbox is that it will now require additional steps for an instructor to create an assignment where grades & feedback are provided to students but the use case calls for the course grade to be not be affected.

The instructor will now need to perform an additional step of editing the Gradebook item to uncheck “Include item in course grade calculations”.

The future of assignments and grading in general is going to be driven by the grading service. For instance, I’m currently looking at specifications grading, which will add extra grading types to the grading service. I expect the assignments grade type dropdown will delegate to the grading service for that list. So, as time goes on we want to simplify the tools, move more and more of their grading logic into the grading service. So, I don’t know what to do with this. It’s a thorny one :)

{noformat}-- Background
-- ----------
-- MFR_PERMISSION_LEVEL_T holds two distinct kinds of rows:
--   (a) Six global defaults (Owner, Author, Nonediting Author, Contributor,
--       Reviewer, None) seeded at startup and loaded by TYPE_UUID at runtime.
--       These are intentionally NOT referenced by any FK.
--   (b) Per-item rows created when a membership item uses the "Custom" level.
--       These MUST be referenced by MFR_MEMBERSHIP_ITEM_T.PERMISSION_LEVEL.
--
-- The bug this script repairs:
--   Lessons' applyGroupRestrictions() changed a membership item's
--   PERMISSION_LEVEL_NAME (e.g. Reviewer -> None) without nulling the
--   PERMISSION_LEVEL FK, leaving the item pointing to a stale level row.
--
-- Two cleanup cases
-- -----------------
-- Case 2 (run first): Any membership item whose PERMISSION_LEVEL_NAME is one
--   of the six standard names should have PERMISSION_LEVEL = NULL.  The app
--   resolves standard-named items via the global defaults at runtime; a per-item
--   FK is redundant and caused the UI to display the wrong level name.
--
-- Case 1 (run second): After nulling the stale FKs, delete any rows in
--   MFR_PERMISSION_LEVEL_T that are no longer referenced AND are not one of
--   the six standard global-default names.  Standard-named unreferenced rows
--   are preserved (they are the global defaults or harmless duplicates that
--   Sakai will simply ignore).

-- ============================================================
-- DIAGNOSTICS -- run these first to preview scope of changes
-- ============================================================

-- Items with a standard level name but a non-null PERMISSION_LEVEL FK (Case 2):
SELECT mi.ID, mi.NAME, mi.PERMISSION_LEVEL_NAME, mi.PERMISSION_LEVEL,
       pl.NAME AS linked_level_name
FROM   MFR_MEMBERSHIP_ITEM_T mi
JOIN   MFR_PERMISSION_LEVEL_T pl ON pl.ID = mi.PERMISSION_LEVEL
WHERE  mi.PERMISSION_LEVEL IS NOT NULL
  AND  mi.PERMISSION_LEVEL_NAME NOT IN ('Custom');

-- Orphaned non-standard permission level rows (Case 1):
SELECT pl.ID, pl.NAME, pl.TYPE_UUID
FROM   MFR_PERMISSION_LEVEL_T pl
WHERE  pl.ID NOT IN (
           SELECT PERMISSION_LEVEL
           FROM   MFR_MEMBERSHIP_ITEM_T
           WHERE  PERMISSION_LEVEL IS NOT NULL
       )
  AND  pl.NAME NOT IN (
           'Owner', 'Author', 'Nonediting Author',
           'Contributor', 'Reviewer', 'None'
       );

-- ============================================================
-- CASE 2: NULL out PERMISSION_LEVEL for standard-named items
-- ============================================================

UPDATE MFR_MEMBERSHIP_ITEM_T
SET    PERMISSION_LEVEL = NULL
WHERE  PERMISSION_LEVEL IS NOT NULL
  AND  PERMISSION_LEVEL_NAME NOT IN ('Custom');

-- ============================================================
-- CASE 1: Delete orphaned non-standard permission level rows
-- ============================================================
-- Run after Case 2 so all stale FKs have already been nulled.
-- Standard-named rows (the six global defaults) are intentionally
-- left in place even if unreferenced.

DELETE FROM MFR_PERMISSION_LEVEL_T
WHERE  ID NOT IN (
           SELECT PERMISSION_LEVEL
           FROM   MFR_MEMBERSHIP_ITEM_T
           WHERE  PERMISSION_LEVEL IS NOT NULL
       )
  AND  NAME NOT IN (
           'Owner', 'Author', 'Nonediting Author',
           'Contributor', 'Reviewer', 'None'
       );{noformat}

{noformat}The portal tool in Sakai implements a sophisticated buffering system for tool rendering. Here's how it works:

  1. Core Buffering Mechanism:
    - BufferedContentRenderResult class in portal-impl captures and holds tool output
    - The bufferContent method in SiteHandler uses a ByteArrayServletResponse to capture tool output before display
    - This allows tools to be rendered inline rather than in iframes when possible
  2. Buffer Bypass Rules:
    - The portal decides whether to buffer using checkBufferBypass method
    - Tools can be exempted from buffering based on:
        - URL patterns (configured via portal.bypass property)
      - Query string patterns (portal.bypass.query)
      - Content type patterns
      - Special AJAX requests (e.g., Wicket AJAX is never buffered)
  3. Rendering Control Flow:
    - First, tools are checked if they can be rendered inline using allowBufferContent
    - JSR-168 portlets are never buffered
    - User permissions for the tool are checked
    - The includeTool method in SkinnableCharonPortal decides final rendering approach
    - Buffered content is processed and parsed to separate head and body sections
  4. Deferred Rendering:
    - Tool content is collected in the SiteHandler.doSite method
    - Actual rendering is deferred until doSendResponse
    - This allows the portal to control the final page assembly

  This architecture improves page load performance by allowing selective tool content buffering while maintaining compatibility with tools that need to be rendered in iframes.{noformat}

I think it makes a lot of sense to have a more granular permission for allowing visibility of the Roster information by role. The scenario where instructors need to see the user ID but students should not see it (while still being able to view the Roster list of names, nicknames, etc.) is a reasonable one. Directory Information can vary school-by-school. If the request is to add a new permission to show/hide the Sakai “User ID” from roles, this seems like a very reasonable request.

Perhaps add the option “View participant’s User ID” after “View participant’s email”?

To be clear, the US Department of Education says that the following information is available/allowable within the context of an online class site (and all students officially enrolled in the same class can see this information freely, even if a FERPA directory hold has been requested):

* Name
* Email address
* Electronic Identifier (often a network username, school ID, or other identifier)

Source: “A student has opted out of directory information and wants to be anonymous in an online course. Are we required to allow the student to take the course anonymously?” _Protecting Student Privacy_, U.S. Department of Education, [https://studentprivacy.ed.gov/faq/student-has-opted-out-directory-information-and-wants-be-anonymous-online-course-are-we-required|https://studentprivacy.ed.gov/faq/student-has-opted-out-directory-information-and-wants-be-anonymous-online-course-are-we-required|smart-link] 

No school should use confidential personal information, such as Social Security Number, as a school ID, username, etc. 

Again, since each school declares its own rules for “directory information,” the “User ID” may or may not be protected information. It depends on how one interprets the definition, “Directory Information is information contained in the education records of a student that would not
generally be considered harmful or an invasion of privacy if disclosed.” (See “[https://studentprivacy.ed.gov/faq/may-educational-agency-or-institution-disclose-directory-information-without-prior-consent|https://studentprivacy.ed.gov/faq/may-educational-agency-or-institution-disclose-directory-information-without-prior-consent|smart-link].“)

The T&L/UX group looked at the Upvoting and Reactions features today, and we agreed that the following modifications would enhance the user experience:

* Change “Bookmark” icon from a star (*y) to a bookmark [https://fontawesome.com/v4/icon/bookmark|https://fontawesome.com/v4/icon/bookmark|smart-link]  
* Change the icons for items that have not been bookmarked or pinned to the “outline” version of the icon, and items that have been bookmarked/pinned to the filled version of the icon. 
** not selected
!image-20241016-162131.png|width=146,height=61,alt="image-20241016-162131.png"!
** selected 
!image-20241016-162421.png|width=161,height=48,alt="image-20241016-162421.png"!
* Use rounded rectangle containers to group the individual upvoting and reaction elements so it is easy to see which items go together.
* Include the labels for “Upvote” and “Add Reaction” so that the meaning of these items is clear to users (also better for accessibility)
* For upvoting, include upvote count and allow students to see the number of upvotes. (Down-voting is not allowed.) 
* Enable upvoting for topics as well as answers/responses.
* Add sorting options for topics to sort by: Upvotes, Most Recent, Oldest, Least Active, Most Active
* Add answer/response sorting option for Upvotes (for both Question and Discussion topics)
* For reactions, use a grayed-out smiley with a plus sign for adding reactions. When this item is clicked, present the user with an emoji selection to choose from. 
** Note: T&L/UX preferred providing the full emoji library selection to give users more choice. The group felt that users should be trusted to select appropriate icons in the same way that they are trusted to compose appropriate text responses. However, we did think that if the full library is allowed, instructors should have the ability to remove student-added reactions in case there is something inappropriate that needs to be addressed.
* Once a reaction has been added, display the emoji icon under the message along with a count of the number of reactions for that icon. Multiple icons are displayed next to each other in the same line, each with a count.
* Remove the separate “Good Post” thumbs up icon and just let it be a part of the set of available reaction emojis. T&L didn’t see a need for singling it out, and it looks cleaner and less confusing without that extra icon and text for each post.

While investigating Safe Exam Browser start-up issues on Sakai 25, we reviewed the commit for this ticket (db3571f8b21, PR #14313). Besides the return URL behaviour described above, it includes several other changes that are not mentioned in the description or the test plan, and that may be relevant to other institutions, especially when considering a backport to 25.x:

# *SEB key validation condition fixed* ({{deliverySafeExamBrowser.js}}). The condition was inverted: with empty keys the page validated immediately, and with keys present (the normal case) it waited for the {{SafeExamBrowser.security.updateKeys}} callback. If that callback never arrives, the student is left on an endless loading spinner. 25.x still has the inverted condition.
# *Start-phase revalidation* ({{DeliveryBean.validate()}}). The secure delivery HTML fragment and {{blockDelivery}} are no longer reset on every call. When the status is FAILURE with an empty fragment (the SEB case), the ASSESSMENT_START phase is validated again. As a side effect, SEB question pages now load the SEB script and send a {{sebValidation}} request on each page.
# *Start-phase error fragment for other modules* ({{DeliveryActionListener}}, {{LinearAccessDeliveryActionListener}}). When a non-SEB secure delivery module (e.g. Respondus) fails the ASSESSMENT_START phase, its HTML fragment is now rendered.
# *Secure delivery editable on published assessments* ({{publishedSettings.jsp}}, {{authoringSecureDeliverySettings.js}}). The secure delivery module and the exit password are no longer disabled in the published assessment settings, so instructors can change or remove the secure delivery requirement after publishing. This is a behaviour change that sites may want to be aware of.
# *Settings form fixes* ({{authoringSecureDeliverySettings.js}}). Enabling or disabling a radio group now affects all its options ({{querySelectorAll}} instead of {{querySelector}}), and SEB-specific settings are hidden when another module is selected.
# *Missing link guard* ({{deliverySafeExamBrowser.js}}). {{configureLink}} no longer fails when the link element is not on the page.
# *Accesskey removed* from the "Return" button on the secure delivery error page.

* SAK-52964: SEB for Windows may expose the {{SafeExamBrowser}} JavaScript API after page scripts run (SEB issue #1443). This is still under investigation.

I look forward to you testing this.  It is pretty cool I think.  However, stub tools are problematic.  When there is an import with no pre-installed / no pre-matched tool it installs a thing I call a “Stub tool”.  Stub tools are LTI 1.1 tools with missing secrets.  If the original tool was an LTI 1.3 tool - the stub tool will still be an LTI 1.1 tool.  In the instructor UI all they see is the stub tool and all they can do is set a key and secret - that will definately not be enough if this needs to be an LTI 1.3 tool.  To reconstitute an LTI 1.3 tool, after import, you have to go in as admin and edit the tool, remove the site ID, change it to an LTI 1.3 tool and provision it - perhaps through dynamic provisioning.  And you need a new security contract with the LTI 1.3 tool provider - you can’t just reuse the one you used in the original server as re-running Dynamic Registration will break the original server.

I know it is inconvenient - but it is the best we can do given that LTI 1.3 tools are admin only.

There is no way to insure that LTI tools exporting and importing between 2 Sakai servers works smoothly is to pre-install the tools in the new server before starting the import.

Also, when you go cross server, lots of stuff will break.  This Jira fixed “within server export / import” which you can test thoroughly.  As soon as you go cross server (i.e. SAK-50927) it fails pretty spectacularly.

(It would be difficult to represent the rubric selections within the rubric itself unless all reviewers agree on a rating, so it makes sense to just have all of the average scores shown in the adjustment column for consistency.) If the instructor releases grades without modifying the rubric, then the average rubric is what students see, with the average score shown for each criterion. This is much more useful than seeing a blank rubric without any feedback, which is what would show if the instructor doesn’t make any changes and simply selects “Release grades” to release all peer review scores. Of course, if the instructor does make any changes to the rubric, then it shows the instructor’s edited rubric selections instead.

[user] If there is an empty Lessons page in the site and a non-empty Lessons page in the archive - the imported content will “take over” the empty Lessons page and there will be no more empty Lessons page in the content.  After the first import the site’s Lessons page will be non-empty and during a second import the Lessons content in the file will be ignored.  In doing the duplicate removal, there is no check beyond the pages in the site and their empty / non empty status.  If for example you have a site with Lessons and one page, and a file with Lessons and 100 pages, the import will not overwrite the site content and will not extend the site content - the imported content (with 100 pages) will treated as duplicate and not ignored.  If you want to import content named Lessons in a file just rename Lessons in the site to something else and then the import will pull in all the content under the Lessons page.  This is to avoid breaking existing content in the site by mashing together two sets of pages and leaving lots of stuff broken.

Hi, thanks for the detailed explanation! This work was initially conceived for a external integration and also with a limited scope as a first step for providing Sakai with a dynamic learning itinerary. Now it’s for the community to use and improve, and we surely love getting proposals to improve it.

Having said that, there are lots of things here: some are UI fixes (we agree the current setup steps can be confusing), some are interesting additions (display info) and other look like desirable extensions (i.e. Gradebook items were never covered by lessons, and we need to consider that tool’s going to be refactored), etc.

For that reason we believe it would be good to split all this into different subtasks and work on defining the specific requirements for each of them. Some might be more complex than others and we believe some bits shouldn’t delay UI improvements from being contributed.

At this point it would be also good to mention that ideally the conditional service and the old linear pre-requisites (which aren’t visually very pretty) shouldn't be mutually exclusive. So not everything can be done now, but maybe it'd be good to at least move forward a design that consideres that path.

As we made the original development we’re going to review this Jira internally and will come up with a proposal to the community regarding subtasks, their priority and the ones we'll be able to work on in the short term.

There are some other minor changes.

The T&L/UX group discussed the proposed UI changes today. The consensus of the the group was in favor of all the changes except for the removal of the site title from the top navigation area. 

In the UX testing that was done prior to 23 release, users very clearly expressed a need for better sense of place in knowing which site they are currently in. Also, having a large empty space at the top was reported by several testers as wasted space that they would rather see filled with useful information. These test results were the rationale for moving the title and tool breadcrumb into that space to begin with. User feedback from institutions using 23 right now also report that faculty tend to get “lost” and forget which course they are in if they scroll down the page and the left nav is not easily visible. Having the title at the top is very helpful in reminding them of which site is selected.

The S2U change in the top nav was prompted by the fact that their institution site titles tend to be quite long and look bad when they overflow the space and push other items to the far right. We recognize that this is an issue, but would like to find a way to mitigate the problem without removing the site title  from the top nav area. T&L/UX suggests that we do the following instead:

* Truncate the site title when it reaches a particular character or space limit (as is currently done on mobile).
* If the Tool breadcrumb is a space issue in the top nav, consider moving the tool name only into the content area Breadcrumb space. (No need to duplicate the title in the breadcrumbs if it appears at the top.)

As mentioned above, the other changes were agreed to be improvements. The group liked limiting the number of expanded site tools on the left. We also thought that presenting the tool options in a dropdown list, instead of tabs which tend to wrap and bunch up at the top, is a much better experience.

I’m not a fan of the Home site moving around in the left nav. I think it should stay fixed to the top of the left nav and just collapse when another site is opened. We did some UX testing on this before 23 came out and several test participants reported that changing the order of sites in the left nav was unexpected and a little confusing. I don’t mind reorienting the left nav to automatically scroll down a bit so the currently selected site displays at the top, but scrolling back up should still reveal the Home site above it. Keeping Home in the top left all of the time gives a better sense of stability to the interface. When the Home site appears to jump around, it looks a bit clumsy.

[user] 

Is the current site expected to be positioned right below Home? Or do you simply want to remove this feature?  

Shifting the view only to the current site might cause confusion, as it could give the impression that there’s nothing else above. Spanish universities discussed this and agreed that the open site should be placed at the top (though keeping Home in the first position is a good idea).  

Another idea is to create an additional section. Currently, we have Home, Pinned, and Recent. It could instead be Home, Current, Pinned, and Recent.  

What do you think the desired behavior should be?

[user] In some of the early iterations of the Trinity portal, we did actually have a Current Site section at the top, under Home. In the usability testing we did, we found that moving the currently selected site to the top was problematic for a few reasons.

For example, if there is a Current section at the top, do you remove the selected site from the list below so that it doesn’t appear twice? We received clear feedback that seeing the same site in the list twice was redundant, so leaving it listed under Pinned/Recent while also at the top was not something users wanted.  

However, if you remove the site from Pinned/Recent to the Current section when you select a site, the sites appear to “jump” from one section to another and back again. Test participants expressed confusion over sites seeming to “jump around” on the screen (moving from Pinned or Recent to Current and back again). They expected/preferred the list of sites to remain in a stable, predictable order. Particularly since they may have deliberately put their pinned sites into a specific order, and may find it harder to locate sites when they don’t appear in that order.

Additionally, we received feedback that the extra space needed for the label Current (and the spacing around it) pushed everything else further down the screen in the left menu. This was undesirable because it required more scrolling and users were already adapting to scrolling up and down to access sites in Pinned, rather than along the top of the screen as in 22.x. Users also thought the Current label was unnecessary, so we ended up removing it.

Based on the testing feedback, I would recommend removing the “move selected site to the top” feature. Or, if the label Current and the site ordering behavior is something that could be configured in sakai.properties by individual institutions, that would be fine as well. However, I would recommend that the default site ordering behavior remain the same as it is in 23.x.

* It would be consistent with how the other tools work with cc+

The cc+ export/import actually works much better than import from site for the tools supported so far, instructors do not have to be in the export site, and if there are dates and it is now a different term, the Date Manager can handle a lot of the date updates. Even if the instructor has to go through each Conversation to change any with dates, it is still less work than trying to figure out what other settings need to be set that depend on dates.

I agree with [user] - I think due dates should be exported/imported so that when you restore the course to a new site, it is as close to the original as possible, which includes due dates and associated settings. Even if the dates are not relevant to the new site, it is still good to know which items in the course were intended to have due dates and where those dates fit into the overall design of the course.

*What we will change:*

# Removed Wicket AJAX behavior - No more setupAccordionBehavior() calls that destroy/recreate DOM elements

* jQuery UI sortable survives - Since the table DOM elements are never destroyed, the sortable behavior remains attached
* Pure client-side - No AJAX requests that could interfere with JavaScript behaviors

  Benefits:

* Better performance - No server round-trips for accordion state
* Preserves all JavaScript behaviors - Sortable, event handlers, etc. stay intact
* Simpler code - Less Java logic, more standard Bootstrap
* State persistence - Accordion state saved across page reloads via localStorage

When you’re tabbing or using the arrow keys in Chrome alone, you’re exercising the browser’s built‑in focus model: every focusable element (links, buttons, form controls) is in the natural DOM order and responds predictably. JAWS, however, sits on top of that and introduces its own modes and key intercepts:
	1.	Virtual Cursor vs. Forms Mode
	•	By default JAWS puts you in “Virtual PC Cursor” mode, where arrow keys read text and move a virtual cursor—focus doesn’t actually land on elements until you switch into Forms/Focus mode (with Enter or F10).
	•	If you try arrow‑key navigation without entering Forms mode, nothing happens to real focus, so your application’s roving tabindex or arrow‑key handlers won’t fire.
	2.	Key Interception
	•	JAWS intercepts many keystrokes (including arrows, Home/End, Page Up/Down) for its own navigation commands. Unless your components expose the correct ARIA roles (e.g. role="menu", aria-activedescendant on role="listbox"), JAWS won’t hand arrow events back to your app.
	3.	ARIA Semantics & Focus Management
	•	Native controls (e.g. <button>, <input>) work seamlessly because JAWS knows their behavior. Custom widgets need full ARIA support—proper roles, focusable container, tabindex="0", and explicit aria-label—so JAWS can map them to its virtual cursor and Forms mode correctly.

A couple of quick points:

a) The hamburger is just an icon. It’s not a “hamburger menu” it’s really a drag handle

b) This component is not using draggable=true so the WINDOWS Key+CTRL+EQUALS to enter the JAWS internal drag-and-drop mode is not useful. This component is using simple keyboard controls: tab to focus on the hamburger icon, then space or enter to select the item, then arrow keys to move the item.

However, I found out that this was not the case for Sakai 23 (and later). Students were obtaining access to content stored Resources, presumably through links. I’m certainly open to a more flexible permissions granting/revoking scheme across folder hierarchies. However, while getting the folder permissions right is important, my bigger concern is that access control, whether through folder permissions or through the ‘Availability and Access’ controls work as an instructor would expect--- granting access and denying access to content as expected.

To clarify the use case I have in mind here, I know of some instructors who store things like answers to assessments within folders in Resources for TAs to access but not students. However, I surmise that partly due to instructor error that there may have been leaks.

*Locking Resources via Site Info > Tool Order:* What should the effect of locking the Resources tool be? Should it be to override all content.read permissions for students regardless of what the permission settings are for the folder that contains the resource? [user] For the use case you noted (allowing TAs to view answer key files in Resources but not allowing students to access them) I think a better way for the instructor to do this is by going to the folder containing the items, using the Actions > Edit Details > Availability and Access settings to select “Hide this folder and its contents.” Since the TA role can read hidden resources by default, this will restrict the folder/files to TAs.

You can accomplish the same thing by going to Actions > Edit Folder Permissions and removing the read.content access for Students at the folder level. However, I would advise against doing this for the root folder in the site, because, as you noted, removing permissions at the top level can sometimes create unforeseen issues. 

As I’m sure you know, making the Resources tool invisible will hide the tool in the menu, but allow site participants to access links to resource items. Locking the Resources tool will restrict site participants from accessing Resources items completely. However, hidden and locked tool menu settings apply to both student and TA roles in a site.

I suppose this is a roundabout way of saying that there are multiple ways of hiding or restricting access to content in a site, and perhaps editing tool permissions directly isn’t always the best method.

While I do support the idea of instructors being able to add/remove permissions in Resources per folder as needed (since that seems to be the expected behavior), I would still caution users to take care when making such changes - particularly if instructors are changing permissions at the root level for the site. In most cases, it is probably better to use other methods (e.g. hiding, locking, or even selective release to groups) for restricting student access to content.

In other words, I would suggest the following:

# Go to *Site Info > Manage Groups*.
# Create a “*TA*” group in the site and add the *Role: Teaching Assistant* role to the group membership.
# Go to *Site Info > Tool Order.*
# Make the *Resources* tool “*invisible to students*” (not locked). This will hide the Resources link in the tool menu for both TAs and students.

## Select *Add Content Link > Select an existing file from Resources* and choose one or more files to add to the page as individual links. ## If you have several links you want to put on the page to do selective release all at once, (or if you prefer to use the *Add Content > Add Resources Folder* option for adding links), then you should first go to *Add Content > Add Subpage*. Once the subpage has been added, edit the subpage item and in the *Visibility and Access* section of the item settings, *Edit the groups for which this item should be shown* and select the *TA* group only. Then, you may add as many items or folder links as you choose to the subpage, and anything on that subpage will be available to TAs only.

I’ve tested this on trunk and it works without any issues for me. By using Lessons to control access using groups, you can completely avoid any outstanding bugs related to controlling access via Resources permissions. 

The only catch is that instructors need to make sure they do not place links to restricted files in any other locations within the course where students can get to them. Likewise, TAs should be aware that they should not share these links with students. As long as those links stay on the selectively released Lessons pages which only TAs can access, then students won’t see the links at all.

T&L/UX looked at this issue today. The group felt that the use of a property was confusing here. It seems as though the property controls the ability to view all students for both instructors and TAs. However, in many cases, the institution may want instructors to see all, but TAs to only see their own groups. This would be more appropriate to control with a permission, rather than a property, so that the permission can be added or removed from the TA role as needed, without affecting the instructor’s ability to view all. 

In our testing, we noticed that the “assessment.gradeAssessment.any” permission seems to be required to grade assessments at all, not just for a user’s own group. 

T&L/UX proposes that we need a new permission for "assessment.gradeAssessment.group" so that TAs can have that permission instead of the assessment.gradeAssessment.any permission to differentiate the view all from view own group.

Also, since Tests & Quizzes does not have a Permissions tab like other tools (e.g. Assignments), it means that any permission change would need to be set by the admin. T&L/UX would like to point out that there is an existing Jira about adding the Permissions tab to T&Q to make modifying this permission easier. [https://sakaiproject.atlassian.net/browse/SAK-50667|https://sakaiproject.atlassian.net/browse/SAK-50667|smart-link]

I have reviewed this PR in relation to the comments from T&L and have concluded that the way this issue should be resolved is to introduce a new samigo permission (that matches assignments)

{noformat}AUTHZ_ASSESSMENT_ALL_GROUPS = "assessment.all.groups";{noformat}

where when this permission is combine with another permission it gives the user access to performing that function on all groups.

The change here fundamentally changes how grading assessments has worked historically and I would propose reverting this change in favor of the approach described by T&L.

This needs to be discussed in the T&L group first.

T&L/UX discussed this today, and the group felt that the change in behavior to reset the category was not a good thing, since it means that instructors will always have to change the category for an item on creation, rather than the way it works in prior versions where they only needed to change the category if it was different than the most recently created item. The group felt that instructors creating several items at once would be forced to make more clicks to accomplish the same task. And, since there is no way to bulk change categories, it is particularly laborious to have to change each one individually in the gradebook if the wrong category is selected. The overall consensus was that one less click per item is better, and keeping the old behavior (not resetting) is preferred. 

Incidentally, we also looked at other tools to see if they reset the category or not, and they do not. For consistency, the group proposed creating a Jira to make it so that other tools do not reset the category each time either.
Given the comments from T&L it sounds like this should be reverted to the previous way it worked, will add this to the core call for resolution.

T&L/UX looked at this issue today, and the consensus of the group is that we do not like the change in behavior. Users are already accustomed to having newly pinned items appear at the bottom of the list. In addition, several of the folks on the call noted that adding items to the top of the list would disrupt the order of their currently pinned sites, making it necessary to reorder items each time to make sure that the ones they have selected to be at the top actually remain there. This is particularly annoying for admins, or faculty with lots of classes, since they may be added to new sites often, including future terms which are not yet available for students and which they may not want to see at the top of the list. 

The T&L/UX group believes this change should either be reverted, or there should be a sakai.property and/or user preference added to allow institutions or individual users to set their own preference for the order of newly pinned items. However, we think the default behavior should remain as it is in Sakai 23, with newly pinned items appearing at the bottom of the pinned sites list.

Instructors often use the same SCORM packages in more than one site, just as they often use assignments or quizzes in more than one site. New copies or instances of assignments and quizzes are always treated as independent, separate items, and so should the SCORM objects.

T&L/UX looked that this issue today, and the group consensus was that non-passing scores should be sent to differentiate from a non-attempt. Also, having a non-passing score sent automatically would eliminate the need for instructors to have to manually zero out the scores. We assume that LTI tools will replace the score if a newer/higher score is generated within the tool by a subsequent attempt.

Sakai doesn’t silently “flip” failed attempts to completed. When the SCO calls Terminate we hand the data model back to the bundled ADL library (SCORM_2004_DM.terminate). That code can derive a completion value only if the SCO has  already supplied both cmi.progress_measure and cmi.completion_threshold; in that case it sets cmi.completion_status to "completed" when progress ≥ threshold or to "incomplete" otherwise (scormplayer/scorm-api/src/java/org/adl/datamodels/
  ieee/SCORM_2004_DM.java:1120-1148). If those values aren’t present—or if the SCO keeps writing "incomplete" after that calculation—the status never changes.
  

There is no Sakai-side logic that promotes a failing score to “passed” or marks a module as completed on its own; ScormApplicationServiceImpl simply reads the final cmi.* values the SCO (or the ADL DM based on the SCO’s inputs) leaves in the data manager.

Here are the most likely lessonbuilder commits that could have introduced this regression (pages newly imported but unvisited show under “not in use” on Index of Pages). All of them alter import/merge or top-level page wiring,
which directly affects whether pages are “reachable” from top-level pages and thus excluded from the “unused” bucket.

Suspects

* SAK-50978 (6732b2067ed): CC+ import refactor. Large rewrite of LessonBuilderEntityProducer merge/import pipeline. Changes how pages are created, when parent/topParent/toolId are set, and when top-level SimplePageItem
“vestigial” items are created. If some top-level or subpage links aren’t written until later or in certain paths, newly imported but unvisited pages would remain “unreferenced,” so PagePickerProducer adds them under “not in use.”
* SAK-51353 (9f034d41752): Merge my data path. Split mergeInternal into transferCopy vs merge flows; changed reuse/empty detection of placements and how items/pages are assigned. Could leave some imported pages without top-level
linkage until visit.
* SAK-51423 (b5ac97735c6): Site copy fixes. Further changes to the same import/merge code paths. If top-level page toolId/parent/item creation isn’t consistently applied across all placements/pages, those pages wouldn’t be
traversed by Index of Pages and would show as “not in use” until later.
* SAK-50802 (1e58a8f5810, then follow-up/revert cycles): Avoid creating Lessons placements with no content; also logic to detect content before creating nav entries. If the content detection misses some pages/items, a placement/
page may exist without the corresponding top-level SimplePageItem, appearing as unused until the tool/page is accessed.
* SAK-48907 (80464b570f5): Restore subpage navigation. Touched LessonsSubNavBuilder, SimplePageToolDao APIs, and portal integration. Less likely than the import changes, but it changed how Lessons page structures are computed and
exposed, which can ripple into PagePickerProducer ordering and detection.

*Why these are relevant*

* Index of Pages classification: PagePickerProducer builds a “graph” starting from top-level page items (getOrderedTopLevelPageItems) and recursively follows PAGE items. Any SimplePage left in pageMap after traversal is displayed
under the “The following pages are currently not in use” header.
* The reported behavior implies imported pages exist in the DB but are not yet reachable from the top-level items. That happens if:
** Top-level SimplePageItem for a placement wasn’t created, or
** The top-level page’s toolId/parent/topParent aren’t set correctly, so it’s not picked up as top-level, or
** Subpage PAGE items on parent pages weren’t created/mapped yet.
* The commits above specifically changed when and how top-level pages/items and PAGE links are created/updated during import and site copy.

*Code pointers*

* PagePickerProducer.java: builds reachable page list from getOrderedTopLevelPageItems(siteId) and marks leftovers as “unused.”
* SimplePageToolDaoImpl.getOrderedTopLevelPageItems(siteId): relies on:
** findItemsInSite(siteId) → findTopLevelPageItemsBySakaiIds(top-level SimplePage.pageIds)
** getTopLevelPages(siteId): SimplePage with parent==null and toolId in site’s pages
** If import leaves toolId/parent unset or no top-level SimplePageItem created, the page won’t be traversed.
* LessonBuilderEntityProducer.java (merge/import): recent refactors (commits listed) added complex logic for:
** Creating or reusing placements
** Creating “vestigial” top-level SimplePageItem for top-level SimplePage
** Setting simplePage.setParent(null)/setTopParent(null)/setToolId(...)
** Creating PAGE items (links) for subpages
** Any missed/conditional path here can cause unvisited imported pages not to be wired into the graph yet.

*Recommended next steps*

* Reproduce on trunk with a site import containing multiple Lessons pages (multiple placements and/or subpages), then inspect DB for:
** Top-level pages having parent=null and toolId set
** Existence of top-level SimplePageItem (pageId=0, type=PAGE, sakaiId=top-level pageId)
** Existence of PAGE items on parent pages for subpages

[user] Use cases:

# Reducing noise in the side menu
## When a course has many Lessons or subpages, the menu can become very long and confusing.
## Hiding secondary pages prevents overwhelming students with too many visible entries, while still keeping the page accessible.
# Supplementary or support content
## Pages can be used for optional material, FAQs, additional resources, etc.
## They don’t take up space in the menu but remain available through links from other parts of the course.
# Assessment scenarios
## A subpage with instructions for a practice, a case study, or an exam can be hidden from the menu.
## Students only access it when the instructor shares the link (e.g., in an announcement or in the assignment description).
# Pilot tests or materials in preparation
## Allows the instructor to prepare a Lessons page that is already accessible via link (for review or testing with selected students) without making it visible in the regular navigation.

[user] [user] [user] I think what’s happening is the following. The copyToolPermissions method in SiteManageServiceImpl that I modified to prevent overwriting all permissions is (and has been) using siteService.save(toSite) to “save permissions”. However, I surmise from what we’re now observing, this approach via SiteService is only changing permissions in memory and not saving said changes to the database.

The Permissions panels (I think) use PermissionsController, which in turn uses AuthzGroupService to save an AuthzGroup for permissions.

I assume this latter approach is needed for SiteManageServiceImpl.copyToolPermissions in place of SiteService.

Update: I hope to have a new PR later this afternoon (US Pacific).

{{SiteManageServiceImpl.copyToolPermissions}} updates each destination role and then calls {{siteService.save(toSite)}}, but no permissions are persisted because Site only saves its realm when the {{m_azgChanged}} flag is set.

The flag never flips during the copy because {{Site.getRole}} merely proxies to the underlying authz group, and the {{Role.allowFunction/disallowFunction}} helpers only mutate an in-memory Set without notifying the site.

As a result, the copy appears to succeed but the database remains unchanged, unlike the permissions UI which explicitly saves via {{AuthzGroupService}}.

Summary of changes in PR

  Schema & Persistence Model                                                                                                                                                                                                                               

* Replaced 4 separator-encoded string fields (DIRECTPARENTIDS, PARENTIDS, DIRECTCHILDIDS, CHILDIDS) on the old HierarchyPersistentNode entity with a self-referential [user] JPA relationship backed by a new HIERARCHY_NODE_PARENTS join table
* Added DDL migration scripts for MySQL, Oracle, and HSQLDB creating HIERARCHY_NODE_PARENTS                                                                                                                                                              
* Added a fixupDatabase() migration that detects and migrates existing encoded-string parent data into the join table, then drops the obsolete columns; column detection uses JDBC metadata to avoid noisy SQL error logging                           

  Entity & Package Restructure                                                                                                                                                                                                                             

* Deleted the old HierarchyPersistentNode, HierarchyNodeMetaData, HierarchyNodePermission DAO model classes and their Hibernate .hbm.xml mapping files                                                                                                   
* Deleted the old HierarchyNode DTO (which existed only to expose decoded Set<String> to callers)                                                                                                                                                        
* Created new HierarchyNode and HierarchyNodePermission JPA entities in org.sakaiproject.hierarchy.model — the package external callers already imported, so no import changes needed outside the module                                                 

  Repository Layer                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         

* Replaced the old HierarchyDao / HierarchyDaoImpl / genericdao pattern with Spring-style HierarchyNodeRepository and HierarchyNodePermissionRepository interfaces backed by SpringCrudRepositoryImpl                                                    
* Added findAllAncestors / findAllDescendants using ANSI WITH RECURSIVE CTEs (replacing manual transitive closure propagation), with HSQLDB-compatible explicit column list syntax                                                                       
* Annotated all read-only repository methods with [user](readOnly = true)                                                                                                                                                                      

  Service (HierarchyServiceImpl)                                                                                                                                                                                                                           

* Rewrote from ~1,177 lines to ~555 lines by removing all encode/decode logic, all manual transitive-closure propagation loops, and the DTO conversion layer                                                                                             
* addNode / addChildRelation / removeChildRelation / removeNode operate directly on the JPA entity graph                                                                                                                                                 
* Bidirectional inverse-side collections kept in sync manually (the mappedBy side is not auto-updated by Hibernate)                                                                                                                                    
* removeNode simplified: clears owning side, removes node from parent's children in memory, deletes — no redundant save, no re-lookup, no refresh                                                                                                        
* All read-only public methods annotated [user](readOnly = true)                                                                                                                                                                                 
* Captured return values from all save() calls; replaced .getId().equals() with .equals() (Lombok generates equals/hashCode on id)                                                                                                                       

  Deleted Dead Code                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        

* HierarchyImplUtils (encode/decode utilities) — deleted entirely                                                                                                                                                                                        
* HierarchyImplUtilsTest — deleted                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
* HierarchyDaoImpl, ResourceFinder — deleted                                                                                                                                                                                                           
* Old HierarchyServiceImplTest (1,512 lines) replaced with a clean rewrite (1,394 lines)                                                                                                                                                                 
* Old spring-hibernate.xml, sakai-hibernate.xml, hibernate-test.xml wire-up files replaced with components.xml and a Spring Java config test class                                                                                                     

  Delegated Access Callers                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 

* HierarchyNodeSerialized: updated constructor to use getters; childNodeIds/parentNodeIds (transitive closure) left as empty sets since pre-computation was removed                                                                                      
* DelegatedAccessSiteHierarchyJob: replaced all direct field access with getters; in-loop child tracking updated to mutate getChildren() so getDirectChildNodeIds() stays consistent

To resolve this issue properly, we need to decide as a community on a fundamental philosophy for how tools interact with content from Resources. Currently, we have a messy hybrid approach causing bugs like this one. We should likely choose an architectural strategy:

h3. Strategy 1: Absolute Resource Authority (Direct Linking)

Tools like Assignments, Announcements, and Lessons do not copy files. They strictly store a reference pointer back to the original file in the Site’s Resources.

* The Rule: If you choose to link a file from Resources, it remains subject to Resources' Access Control Lists (ACLs), quotas, and visibility states at all times.
* Downstream Impact: If an instructor changes a folder to "hidden with no access" or deletes the resource, that restriction or breaking change immediately applies to the tool using it.
* Note that uploads from students for example in the case of Assignments always go to the tools private storage

h3. Strategy 2: Tool Isolation (Private Storage Copies)

When a file from Resources is attached to a tool, it is completely duplicated into the tool's private storage space inside ContentHosting ({{/attachments/}}).

* The Rule: Once copied, the file cuts all ties with the original Resource folder. The tool becomes solely responsible for maintaining its own ACLs on that {{/attachments/}} collection based on the tool's lifecycle (e.g., if a student has access to view the Assignment, they have access to view the attached file, regardless of what happens to the original folder in Resources).
* This might also add a level of confusion as users (Instructors) probably won’t understand that tools are maintaining separate copies of these files.
* Current Alignment & Downstream Impact: 
** Choosing this strategy means we would need to refactor Lessons to copy files into its own {{/attachments/}} path rather than using direct linking, and Lessons would have to manage its own contextual access control lists going forward.
** Assignments and Announcements already function this way. However, it requires ensuring that each tool explicitly updates and modifies its respective {{/attachments/}} resource properties in ContentHosting to accurately mirror the tool's current visibility states. For example when an instructor changes the visibility of a tool or removes the tool from the site.

Which strategy do we want to commit to as the standard moving forward?
[user] How long has the existing behavior been present? I believe our existing strategy is working fine for the majority and a major rewrite here is likely a mistake.
[user] I am simply asking do we do it the Lessons way (links to resources, which follows resources ACL’S) or the Assignments/Announcements way (Copies which has nothing to do with resources ACL’s)?

The third approach would be to keep them as-is (the hybrid approach). 

This means we wouldn’t reconcile these discrepancies between the tools. If we go this route, the behavior in Assignments and Announcements (where the copy bypasses the original folder's ACL) would be accepted as intended. 

The only actual fix for this JIRA would be local to individual tools, specifically fixing the embedded PDF issues so they behave similarly as the files in the respective tools.

That means the core ACL issue described in this Jira would not be addressed.

It seems that we have finally found the culprit of the issue. Our production Tomcat version is 9.0.106 and it provides a new filter for multi-part requests, limiting the number and size of parts. This was reported in [SAK-51628|https://sakaiproject.atlassian.net/browse/SAK-51628].

It seems that Safe Exam Browser increases the number of parts, specially in one-page assessments with many questions. Answering many questions exceeds the number of allowed parts and, when clicking on Save, the request is rejected without any warning and the answers are not saved.

We have increased the number of parts to 100 and it doesn't fail anymore, though some research should be done to adjust this number.

The other issue, the negative numbers in timer, still happens. I will contribute a patch.

*My Question:* Did you add peer entries to package.json so when you regenerate package-lock, the peer stuff is not lost?

*From AI:*

The {{"peer": true}} entries showed up because of changes in npm, not in your project.

*What changed: npm 7 (Feb 2021)*

* *npm 6 and earlier*: Peer dependencies were not auto-installed. npm warned about unmet peers but didn’t add them to the tree or the lock file, so there were no {{"peer": true"}} entries.

* *npm 7+*: npm started auto-installing peer dependencies and recording them in the lock file with {{"peer": true}}.

*lockfileVersion*

* *Version 2* (npm 5–6): No peer metadata in the lock file.

* *Version 3* (npm 7+): Includes the {{"peer"}} field and the new dependency layout.

*How that affects your project*

{{package-lock.json}} has {{"lockfileVersion": 3}}, so it was generated with npm 7+ and can include {{"peer": true}}. Conflicts appeared because:

# One side was created with an older npm (or an older lockfileVersion).

# The other side was generated with npm 7+ and has the new metadata.

Different npm versions can also change other fields (e.g. {{"license"}}), which added to the conflicts.

So the shift comes from upgrading to npm 7+ and its lock file format, not from anything you added to {{package.json}}.

*A scenario for the proposed change in this jira:* An instructor is teaching 40 students. 20 in Group 1 meet only on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. The other 20 in Group 2 meet on Tuesday and Thursday. Therefore, all their assessments in Tests & Quizzes have separate due dates, etc. but are otherwise identical. The instructor creates Quiz 1 for Group 1. To create Quiz 1 for Group 2, the simplest method would be to duplicate the Quiz 1 - Group 1 draft. In doing so, 26.x quietly changes the RELEASED TO value to 'Entire Site'. Not warned about this happening (or any need to change the group) the instructor forgets to alter the RELEASED TO and related values and just renames the assessment to "Quiz 1 - Group 2" and then publishes. Now Group 1 students are confused about which assessment to take. Some take the Group 1 quiz and some take the Group 2 quiz. Also, the Gradebook likely needs attention given this inadvertent mix-up.

All of this is to say is that the error as presented in Sakai 22/23 is beneficial for instructors to pay attention to the group settings (i.e., add the intended group) before publishing. 

Arguably, the error message in English could use some better/clearer wording. It currently states: “Students are not able to take this assessment because the groups it was released to have been deleted. You must publish a new copy of this assessment.”  That error message might be better worded as: “This assessment’s Settings are configured to be released to groups, but no groups are currently selected. Settings must be revised before this assessment can be published.”

However the stack trace shows that it did happen, after looking at this here is my opinion of the issue: the entity comparison happens in the listener _outside_ any transaction, hibernate is not tracking the assessment entity, and when the service is called to save the assessment changes it opens a new transaction however the assessment entity is detached (i.e. it is not tracked in the persistence context). 

!image-20260325-175051.png|width=731,alt="image-20260325-175051.png"!


Here is how it should be the key difference is where responsibility is divided:

*JSF listener* - owns only UI concerns: binding, validation, and delegating. It passes _form data_ (plain values) to the service, never an entity it fetched itself.

*Service method* - owns everything database-related. It opens (or joins) a transaction, fetches the fresh entity _within that same session_, does the comparison, applies changes, and commits. Hibernate tracks the entity the entire time, so any changes to the entity are known (2nd level cache and dirty reads) keep entities consistent.

h4. [ANNOUNCEMENT] HttpComponents Client 5.6 GA Released
The Apache HttpComponents project is pleased to announce 5.6 release of
HttpComponents HttpClient.

This is the first GA release in the 5.6 release series. It adds several
features such as transport content decompression and content
compression for the async transport, support for Unix sockets,
experimental support for SCRAM-SHA-256 authentication scheme, and
Micrometer/OTel observations & metrics.

Commons Compress, Brotli codec, and ZStd codec are optional
dependencies and get wired into the execution pipeline only if present
on the classpath.

Notable changes and features included in the 5.6 series:

* Unix domain socket support.
* Support for pluggable content codecs via Commons-Compress in the
classic transport. (optional).
* Support for transparent content decompression and content compression
with {{deflate}},{{gzip}}, {{zstd}} (optional), and {{brotli}} (optional)
codecs in the async transport.
* Micrometer/OTel observations & metrics (optinal).
* Off-lock connection disposal by the classic pooling connection
manager. Experimental.
* SCRAM-SHA-256 authentication scheme (RFC 7804). Experimental.
* Request Priority support (RFC 9218). Experimental.
* OFFLOCK connection pool concurrency policy. Experimental.

Compatibility notes:

* As of this version, HttpClient uses BUILTIN
HostnameVerificationPolicy by default, delegating host verification to
JSSE security manager. One must explicitly configure the TLS strategy
to continue using the hostname verifier shipped with HttpClient.
* Five-second TCP keep-alive is now enabled by default.

Hi guys, just wondering if you're aware of this: [https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access|https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access|smart-link] 
If you're not aware, in Chrome 142 greater restrictions have been placed on the type of communication the browser can do over a local network (or what chrome thinks is a local network, e.g. when split DNS is used)

You can work around this issue by using a browser other than chrome, by setting a flag in the chrome settings, or by adding the {{allow="local-network-access"}} attribute to the LTI iframe.

Hi [user] ,

With S2U-32 (and S2U-28) we did not create the Tag Service itself. Our work was limited to extending tag support to the Assignments and Private Messages tools.

These are the properties currently available in sakai.properties:

{noformat}# If the tag service will be enabled or not. (default is true)
# tagservice.enabled

# S2U-32 and S2U-28 Allow the use of tags in some tools: assignments, private messages (default is true)
# tagservice.enable.integrations

# Allow the use of tags in samigo in the authoring part(default is false)
# samigo.author.usetags

# Allow the use of tags in samigo in the authoring part(default is false)
# samigo.author.usetags

# Allows the instructors to delete tags from a question. (default is true)
# samigo.author.allowDeleteTags

# Allow the display of tags in the grading part (default is false)
# samigo.evaluation.usetags

# MULTI-TAGS PROPERTIES
# If true, the tags will be updated in all the questions identical to the one edited (same hash). (default is false)
# If this is enabled, it has preference over the value in samigo.author.multitag.singlequestion.check, so no check will appear to the user and the tags will be updated in any case. (Note: The admin user will always view the check)
# samigo.author.multitag.singlequestion

# If true, the tags will be updated in all the questions identical to the one edited (same hash) based on a check in the interface. (default is false)
# If samigo.author.multitag.singlequestion is true it has preference over this one, so the check won't appear to the user and the saving in all the same hash questions will happen always.
# If both samigo.author.multitag.singlequestion and samigo.author.multitag.singlequestion.check are false,
# the tags will be independent in every question and saving one question won’t affect any other question.
# samigo.author.multitag.singlequestion.check{noformat}

In addition, there is a role permission:

{noformat}tagservice.manage{noformat}

Without this permission, users cannot create tags, they can only view existing ones. Students should not have this permission.

Therefore, to use tags in Assignments, the following are required:

# tagservice.manage permission (instructors).

# tagservice.enabled=true.

# tagservice.enable.integrations=true.

In the 25.x branch, the Tag Service is disabled at the kernel level. To enable it, sakai.tagservice must be removed from the following property in kernel/component-manager/src/main/bundle/org/sakaiproject/config/kernel.properties:

{noformat}[email]=sakai.meetings,microsoft.mediagallery,microsoft.collaborativedocuments,sakai.scorm.singlepackage.tool,sakai.tagservice,sakai.scorm.tool{noformat}

Otherwise, tags cannot be used.

Regarding the Tag Service tool itself, it is not required to have this tool enabled in order to use tags. It is simply a management tool for administering tags.

I've also attached a short guide that I wrote in 2024 about the Tag Service tool and how tags are used across the different tools. The guide is in Spanish, but I hope it will still be helpful for the QA team. The integration has evolved since I wrote that guide, so some of the information may no longer be fully aligned with the current implementation. Please keep that in mind when using it as a reference.

h1. 🧠 Why This Happens (Most Likely Causes)

Nightly Sakai environments often have incomplete or experimental configurations, so several common issues can trigger this error:

h3. *1. The Service Worker file is missing or not accessible*

If the script URL returns:

* 404 Not Found
* 500 Internal Server Error
* A login page instead of JS
* A redirect

…the browser aborts registration.

h3. *2. Wrong MIME type*

Browsers require Service Worker scripts to be served as:

Code

{noformat}Content-Type: application/javascript
{noformat}

If the server sends HTML or text/plain instead, registration fails.

h3. *3. HTTPS or certificate issues*

Service Workers require a secure context. Nightly servers often use:

* Self‑signed certificates
* Certificates that aren’t trusted by the browser

Chrome/Edge may silently block Service Worker registration in these cases.

h3. *4. The script contains invalid JavaScript*

If the Service Worker file has:

* Syntax errors
* Unsupported features
* Early exceptions

…the browser aborts registration.

h3. *5. Scope mismatch*

The script is at the root ({{/}}), which is normally fine, but if the registration code tries to set a scope the browser considers invalid, it will abort.

h1. 🛠️ How to Fix It

Here are the practical steps to resolve the issue:

h2. ✔️ 1. Check whether the Service Worker script loads

Open this URL directly in the browser:

Code

{noformat}https://trunk-maria.nightly.sakaiproject.org/sakai-service-worker.js
{noformat}

If you see:

* A 404 page
* A login page
* HTML instead of JavaScript

→ The file is not being served correctly.

h2. ✔️ 2. Verify the MIME type

In DevTools → Network tab:

* Reload the page
* Click {{sakai-service-worker.js}}
* Check the *Response Headers*

It must be:

Code

{noformat}Content-Type: application/javascript
{noformat}

If not, update the server configuration (Tomcat, Apache, Nginx) to serve {{.js}} files correctly.

h2. ✔️ 3. Confirm the script is valid JavaScript

Open the file and check for:

* Syntax errors
* Missing event listeners ({{install}}, {{activate}}, {{fetch}})
* Code that throws exceptions on load

h2. ✔️ 4. Check HTTPS and certificate validity

If the nightly server uses a self‑signed certificate, the browser may block Service Worker registration.

Fix options:

* Trust the certificate locally
* Or disable Service Worker registration in non‑production builds

h2. ✔️ 5. Disable Service Worker registration in nightly/dev environments

If Sakai doesn’t need offline caching in nightly builds, wrap the registration code:

javascript

{noformat}if (location.hostname === 'trunk-maria.nightly.sakaiproject.org') {
    // Skip service worker registration in nightly environments
} else if ('serviceWorker' in navigator) {
    navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sakai-service-worker.js');
}
{noformat}

This prevents noisy errors during development.

h1. 📌 Summary

The error means the browser tried to register a Service Worker but aborted because the script could not be properly loaded or validated. The most common causes are:

* Missing or inaccessible {{sakai-service-worker.js}}
* Wrong MIME type
* HTTPS/certificate issues
* Invalid JavaScript in the Service Worker file

Fixing the script availability and server configuration will resolve the issue.

this config uses {{PropertyPlaceholderConfigurer}} to wire the desired Provider which can't be achieved when using [user]

There is no due date in LTI.  There is acceptEndDate and submissionEndDate - since LTI has no Due date most tools ask for submissionEndDate and then label that as “Due Date” in the tool. TII Selects Tool Due Date → sends LTI Response with submissionEndDate → sakai receives LTI resonnse and sets Sakai Due Date → Sakai does an LTI Launch and sends Due data as submissionEndDate → TII receives submissionEndDate and displays it in their UI as UI Due Date

SAK-50758 LTI Stealthed Tools When removed should be gone (#13114) from December 17, 2024.

  That change made getTool(...) hide global stealthed tools from a site unless the tool had an explicit lti_tool_site deployment row. That was meant to make removed stealthed deployments disappear, but it changed the behavior for existing links.

  The bug had two parts:

# Existing LTI content links often only have lti_content.tool_id; they do not necessarily have a matching lti_tool_site deployment row. After the tool is changed to visible=stealth, getTool(toolKey, siteId) returns null, so Assignments/Lessons/tool-link UI
treat the item as deleted or misconfigured.
# The new admin-created link path already had code intended to auto-deploy a stealthed tool to the target site, but it used visible.equals(LTI_VISIBLE_STEALTH). visible is a Long; LTI_VISIBLE_STEALTH is an int, so Long.equals(Integer) is always false. That
meant new stealthed tool links also failed to create the deployment row.

Stepping back on the naming and explainer-text points (#3–#5): I'm genuinely happy to keep going back and forth on names and notes, but I'd love to get the _functionality_ out in front of real folks sooner rather than later. Here's my thinking on why it looks the way it does:

The hard part of this problem is that every academic calendar is different, and even within one calendar every instructor lays their schedule out differently. So rather than chase a single "right" flow, the goal here is to offer *several different ways to get at basically the same result* — and let people reach for whichever one matches how _they_ think about their term. I doubt there's a one-size-fits-all layout that'll click for most folks; but once you know how you build your own schedule and you see the options now on offer (beyond just the old mass-shift vs. edit-every-cell), I think a lot of people will quickly work out how to combine a couple of these tools to get done faster than before.

On the *fixed-day Shift calculator specifically (#2):* you're right that nobody knows the exact integer offhand — that's exactly the itch I was scratching. Before this, I'd either (a) eyeball a guess and nudge it +/- until it got close, then fix stragglers cell by cell, or (b) pop open a datediff on the command line to get the real number. So I just built that second one in. The raw "shift by X days" is really there as a *legacy / easy-mode* path for anyone who truly just needs it — my guess (unverified!) is most people will use it to get _close_ and then jump into the other tools to zero in, which is still way less tedious than copy/pasting individual cells.

Totally open to more feedback, and I don't think this is the final form — but I do think what's here is a real step up from where we were, and we can keep building on it. For the handful of schedules I personally manage, I already know the current version is going to save me a ton of time and frustration every quarter. 🙂

T&L/UX reviewed this Jira. We really like the new options for bulk editing of dates! The “fit dates to term” option is particularly nice, especially with the “snap dates” option that maintains the same day of the week during date shifts. 

The UI is improved from earlier iterations, but we would also like to see a few more tweaks. T&L/UX group recommended changes are:

* Make the “Edit Individual Items” tab the default landing page for the tool. 
** Rationale: Instructors are accustomed to seeing the list of all items from a single screen when selecting Date Manager. They may expect/prefer to be able to view the existing dates in a summary screen, particularly if they are teaching a course that was designed by someone else (e.g. a master course or template site) and are unfamiliar with the cadence of due dates. Additionally, having the Bulk options as a separate tab is more consistent with other tools in Sakai where bulk editing options exist (e.g. Gradebook, Lessons). 
* Remove the “Apply to:” list of checkboxes on the “Set dates from milestones” option, as they are redundant in that screen.
* Make the Export/Import buttons in the top right more visible as buttons when not hovered over - i.e. add shading or an outline to indicate that they are buttons, not just text. Currently, they fade away into the background too easily.
* Include more space and/or visual break of some kind at the bottom, between the “Apply” buttons and the “Save Changes” buttons to better differentiate that the buttons at the bottom are for actions across tabs and not just part of the currently selected tab.
* Restyle the “Bulk Edit” and “Edit Individual Items” tabs to match tab styling (buttons) used elsewhere in Sakai to maintain consistency across tools. 
* Column grouping in milestone view: add shading or borders to visually separate tool groups (e.g. Tests vs. Quizzes) to reduce visual overload

While having tight video integration is incredibly valuable for a modern learning environment, trying to build or include a native video processing and hosting infrastructure directly inside an LMS would not be recommended.

An LMS is designed to be a learning management system, not a specialized media streaming platform. Processing, transcoding, and delivery of high-definition, adaptive-bitrate video require completely different architecture, massive server resources, and entirely separate scaling logic.

Rather than bloating the core codebase of the LMS with heavy media-handling infrastructure, the industry-standard approach is to integrate seamlessly with dedicated media platforms. Whether that integration is built natively into the interface or connected via an external protocol (like LTI), leveraging specialized video infrastructure is the only logical and sustainable way to handle media without degrading the core LMS performance.

Historically, Canvas Studio (formerly known as _Arc_) is a *legacy add-on* that institutions must purchase separately from the core Canvas Learning Management System (LMS). Under the hood, Canvas Studio is a standalone platform hosted on its own separate infrastructure and URLs. It connects to your courses using standard *LTI (Learning Tools Interoperability)* protocols, much like Zoom, Turnitin, or Panopto. In fact, administrators can even log into a standalone Studio site completely independent of the Canvas LMS.
