In its default configuration, the tool is simply an organizational and pedagogical layer on top of videos that are already stored in Sakai Resources. If an institution is already uploading videos to Resources and embedding them in Lessons, then adopting this tool does not fundamentally change its storage or processing requirements.

The optional transcoding and adaptive streaming features are intended as an enhancement for institutions that want to improve the end-user experience. Even then, the processing is performed asynchronously and could be delegated to dedicated servers if required, keeping the LMS application nodes isolated from that workload.

One of Sakai's historical strengths has been that institutions retain control over their infrastructure and are not forced into recurring per-user or per-view licensing models. While external platforms such as Kaltura, Panopto, or Canvas Studio are excellent solutions, they often introduce additional licensing and operational costs. This proposal aims to provide a native alternative for institutions that prefer to remain within the Sakai ecosystem while still benefiting from modern video management capabilities.

Institutions that prefer external media platforms can continue using them. This proposal simply expands the available options rather than replacing existing approaches.

In fact, Opencast is an amazing, robust ecosystem for institutions that have the massive infrastructure and specialized DevOps teams required to maintain its distributed multi-node clusters.

However, from a product strategy perspective, looking at this solely through the lens of core code maintenance introduces a dangerous paradox for Sakai's survival in the current market.

If we strictly follow the logic that anything complex or non-core should be delegated via LTI to avoid codebase bloat, we could just as easily deprecate Samigo (since there are dozens of commercial LTI assessment tools), remove native SCORM support, or entirely drop Forums (and Conversations since Conversations never fully replaced Forums due to missing features and migration hurdles, yet we still maintain it). Every time Sakai chooses easy core maintenance over native, out-of-the-box value, we are exponentially shifting the financial and operational burden onto the institutions.

While Canvas has eaten the market, Moodle keeps growing, and Open edX is gaining massive traction by offering rich, native-feeling multimedia experiences, Sakai risks staying frozen in the past. This is exactly why our proposal conceives this tool from the ground up to be completely modular. Based on our direct contact with various institutions, our vision is to establish a foundational framework where video processing and storage are strictly decoupled.

The initial core proposal includes a lightweight, native processing provider leveraging FFmpeg (an industry-standard open-source solution). This is a deliberate strategic choice designed to serve as a zero-config, out-of-the-box option for smaller or medium-sized institutions that cannot afford the high licensing costs of commercial video tools, nor even dream of deploying and maintaining a massive, complex system like Opencast. Because the architecture is envisioned as strictly decoupled, the core of Sakai remains completely safe from heavy lifting; the local FFmpeg engine is just one interchangeable backend provider.

Our proposed for the roadmap:

Since the backend handles storage and processing via abstract providers, we could absolutely include an OpencastProvider in the tool's roadmap. This would allow large universities to route the heavy lifting to their existing Opencast clusters, while still using our tool as the native, cohesive pedagogical front-end within Sakai.

We need to listen to what the community and potential clients are actually asking for. If we don’t provide native, modern utilities that make Sakai competitive today (and if Sakai continues without a market-disrupting plan to attract new users... but that is a story for another time), it won't matter how easy the core codebase is to maintain, because there won't be any institutions left using it. * If the checkbox is not selected:

Deliberately marking it draft: I want to flag up front that this may need considerably more work to be sure it doesn't break other delivery flows, and I'm genuinely not certain this approach is the right fit for Sakai's security model — enforcing at the delivery bean/listener layer versus somewhere more central is exactly the kind of thing I'd like reviewers to weigh in on. A few specific open questions are in the PR description (is "Immediate Feedback only during a take" the correct policy, the user-visible change to post-deadline retakes, whether there are other take entry points that need the same gate, and whether automated coverage should be added given these methods currently have no unit harness).

Noting a related, *lower-severity* delivery-side item that the draft PR (#14736) deliberately does *not* cover, so it's tracked and can be decided separately.

*What the PR fixes:* feedback _content_ (correct answers, question-level feedback) no longer surfaces during an active take for "on specific dates" delivery — gated on Immediate Feedback in {{getShowFeedbackLink()}} and {{setFeedbackMode()}}.

*What it does not fix:* the student's _earned score_ can still appear in the Table of Contents during a take of a by-date assessment once the (base) feedback date has passed. This travels a different path than the content flag:

* {{SectionContentsBean.getPointsDisplayString()}} / {{ItemContentsBean.getPointsDisplayString()}} render earned points gated on {{showStudentQuestionScore}}, not on {{delivery.feedback}}.
* {{DeliveryActionListener.setShowStudentQuestionScore()}} sets that flag from {{isFeedbackOnDate()}}, which {{BeginDeliveryActionListener}} computes from the base {{AssessmentAccessControl.getFeedbackDate()}}. Extended-time exceptions carry no feedback date of their own ({{ExtendedTime}} has only start/due/retract), so an exception holder still within their extended window but past the base feedback date has the base date checked, not their extended one.

*Why it's lower severity / left out of the PR:*

* It's a _score_, not the answer key — much weaker than the content leak.
* Exploitability depends on navigation: with linear navigation (can't revisit) the student can't act on it; only flexible navigation would let them go back and adjust.
* On a correctly configured assessment the authoring-side guard (SAK-34476) forces the feedback date past every deadline _including exceptions_, so {{isFeedbackOnDate()}} is false during any legitimate take and no score shows. The residual is legacy/misconfigured assessments only.

*Important distinction (to avoid over-fixing):* this is separate from two intended behaviors that must NOT change —

# The "Display Scores" setting ({{displayScoreDuringAssessments}}) that shows each question's _point value_ during a take is benign and unrelated.
# *Immediate Feedback* legitimately shows correct/incorrect and the running score as the student goes; that is intended when the instructor selects it and is fully preserved.

If the team decides to close this too, the fix would be a targeted guard that suppresses the earned score only for *non-immediate* takes ({{TAKE_ASSESSMENT}} / {{TAKE_ASSESSMENT_VIA_URL}}), leaving Immediate Feedback and the point-value display untouched. Happy to add it to this PR or a follow-up depending on how you'd like to scope it.

* Invalid input is reported per-student and no longer 500s.
* Message banners are classed by severity, so a successful "Applied to N" shows as success (green) rather than an error.

And yes, to your question from the 21st: there should absolutely be a visible difference. Guo was right that they'd become indistinguishable, and it affected light mode as well as dark.

*What happened:* #14750 fixed the dark-mode blowout by deleting the page-level {{.disabled { background-color:#f1f1f1 }}} rule _and_ stripping the {{disabled}} class off the three {{h:inputTextarea}} tags in {{totalScores.jsp}}. Nothing in the skin styles a bare disabled {{input}}/{{textarea}}, so the "Requires student submission" boxes lost their only affordance. The old {{#f1f1f1}} was a real grey wash against {{--sakai-background-color-1}} (white in light mode), which is why light mode regressed too.

*Fix:* broaden Samigo's existing {{.disabled.awesomplete}} rule to key on the {{:disabled}} attribute instead of a class, plus the muted-text + {{not-allowed}} cursor treatment already used for disabled {{.select}}. Keying on {{:disabled}} covers both sort states — pre-sort the textareas carry {{styleClass="awesomplete"}}, post-sort they carry no class at all, which is exactly why Guo only saw it after sorting by Comments.

*Verified* on a running Sakai 26 build (published assessment, 18 of 50 students submitted, so both variants render together): 32 disabled + 18 editable textareas, identical before and after sorting. Contrast of {{--sakai-text-color-disabled}} on the row background clears WCAG AA in all four states — dark 6.54:1 plain / 5.03:1 striped, light 5.25:1 / 4.75:1.

*Update after tracing the Sakai UI flow*

The original failure was partly caused by the test harness not completing the browser side of the LTI dynamic registration flow. Sakai's tool edit page listens for this message from the registration iframe:

{code:js}window.parent.postMessage(JSON.stringify({ subject: 'org.imsglobal.lti.close' }), '*'){code}

When Sakai receives {{org.imsglobal.lti.close}}, it calls {{/imsblis/lti13/get_registration?key=<tool id>}}, imports the stored dynamic registration JSON into the visible External Tools form, closes the modal, and asks the admin to review and save. If the user closes the iframe manually with the X, that import step does not run and the visible form fields remain blank.

The harness has been fixed and redeployed to send that close message automatically on successful registration and to show a fallback *Return to platform* button that sends the same message manually:

* Harness endpoint: https://lti-conformance-harness.ottenhoff-1f2.workers.dev

So the remaining Sakai  concern is narrower: dynamic registration completion depends on a fragile client-side iframe message plus a separate final admin save. Closing the modal manually silently skips the import step, which makes it look like dynamic registration succeeded but no LTI 1.3 tool fields were applied.

Hi [user],

Thanks for pointing out the historical context in SAK-42953 and PR #7745!

We reviewed the discussion in PR #7745. The reason {{ISO-8859-1}} was introduced there was because Excel on Windows defaults to local ANSI/ISO-8859-1 when opening a CSV file *if no UTF-8 Byte Order Mark (BOM) is present*, which caused accented characters in European languages to look mangled.

However, hardcoding {{ISO-8859-1}} completely breaks non-Latin and extended scripts (such as Turkish {{ğ, ş, ı, İ}}, Arabic, Japanese, Chinese, Cyrillic, etc.), turning those characters into question marks ({{???}}) during CSV export.

In our PR (#14783), we solve *both* problems simultaneously:

# We use {{StandardCharsets.UTF_8}} so all international characters are preserved correctly.
# We explicitly prepend the *UTF-8 BOM (*{{\\uFEFF}}) ({{fstream.write(BOM);}}) to the output stream.

With the UTF-8 BOM present, Microsoft Excel on Windows immediately detects the file as UTF-8 and displays Spanish/French accented characters ({{á, é, ñ}}) correctly, while also preserving Turkish and all non-Latin Unicode characters properly. This provides a universal fix for all locales.

Reviewed the current source at commit ffcb1c7713e. The reported N+1 behavior is not present in the methods identified by this issue:

* BaseAuthzGroupService delegates both methods directly to storage.
* DbAuthzGroupService.getUsersIsAllowed builds one bulk SQL query across the supplied realms and calls dbRead once. Its loop only populates query parameters.
* DbAuthzGroupService.getAuthzGroupsIsAllowed likewise calls dbRead once, with an IN clause when realms are supplied. There is no per-user or per-group database query loop inside this method.
* Neither method uses authzUserGroupIdsCache. That cache serves getAuthzUserGroupIds, and its invalidation is triggered by authorization-group change events rather than these bulk lookups.

Git history shows that the bulk-query structure predates this report by many years. The ticket contains no SQL traces, timings, or profiling evidence to support the claimed reduction of 5,000+ queries per request.

Closing because the proposed optimization is already present and the reported bottleneck is not substantiated. This assessment is based on source inspection, not a large-course benchmark. If a specific tool repeatedly calls these methods, or enrollment updates cause measurable cache churn, please reopen with the affected version, exact reproduction, call stack, query counts, and timings so that the actual bottleneck can be investigated.

First of all, thank you very much for resolving and merging SAK-52772 (PR #15134)! Eliminating the N+1 `isRoleViewType` checks at the Kernel level makes a tremendous difference for large course sites.

As a companion issue discovered during our performance profiling on large sites (5,000+ to 10,000+ enrolled students), GradebookNG exhibits a very similar secondary N+1 query bottleneck when rendering grades and student matrix views:

# **QuickEntryPage:** Iterating through all students individually executes separate queries for grades, comments, and excuses, producing thousands of sequential database round-trips (~14,700 queries for ~4,900 students). We addressed this by pre-fetching via `getGradesForStudentsForItem()` in a single bulk API call before rendering.

# **GradebookPage / Matrix:** Checking student course grade comments (`setHasCourseGradeComment`) sequentially inside the grid builder loop causes thousands of additional queries, which can be cleanly resolved using a bulk fetch into a `Set<String>` before populating the matrix.

I investigated this on our Sakai 25 fork and can confirm the root cause and that it's not a 25.0→25.3 regression — it predates 25.0 itself.

The bug was introduced in commit {{8d314ece4c}} (SAK-49673, #12403, March 2024), which changed the three {{SakaiScript}} call sites ({{copySiteContent}}, {{copySiteContentForTool}}, {{copyResources}}) to pass {{Collections.EMPTY_LIST}}/{{Collections.EMPTY_MAP}} instead of {{new ArrayList<>()}}/{{new HashMap<>()}}. Those collections are immutable, but {{SiteManageServiceImpl.importToolsIntoSite}} unconditionally calls {{toolIds.clear()}} when {{site.setup.import.addmissingtools}} is {{true}} (the default), which throws {{UnsupportedOperationException}}. This commit already predates the {{25.0}} tag, and the same broken code is still present on current {{master}} — no fix exists yet anywhere.

Workaround confirmed working in production: set {{site.setup.import.addmissingtools=false}} in {{sakai.properties}}. With that flag off, the offending code branch (including the {{.clear()}} call) never executes, and the SOAP web service works correctly — you'll just need to ensure destination tools are already present before importing content, since auto-adding missing tools won't happen.

Proper fix should be replacing {{Collections.EMPTY_LIST}}/{{EMPTY_MAP}} with mutable {{new ArrayList<>()}}/{{new HashMap<>()}} at the three call sites in {{SakaiScript.java}}.

  JSON library consolidation

instanceof pattern matching now recovers typed values with zero casts anywhere.

h3. Recent Changes in Sakai Trunk (Assignments / All-Purpose Items)

This issue is directly tied to the introduction and refactoring of *Assignment Supplement Items / All-Purpose Items* (and their associated access control records) in Sakai Assignments ({{AssignmentSupplementItemServiceImpl.java}} and {{AssignmentAction.java}}).

Specifically, recent refactoring or commits in trunk modified how access controls for supplement items are saved:

# *Missing Check-Before-Insert or* {{MERGE}}*/*{{UPSERT}} *Logic*:
#* When editing or re-saving an existing assignment (or when duplicate access rules are submitted via the UI form during {{post_save_assignment}}), {{saveAllPurposeItemAccess()}} calls {{saveOrUpdate()}} without purging existing access records or properly handling existing mappings.
#* Instead of updating an existing access rule for {{admin}} on item {{31}}, the service attempts to insert a brand new {{AssignmentAllPurposeItemAccess}} entity with the same unique composite key.
# *Transaction boundary & Session Reuse issue*:
#* In {{AssignmentAction.saveAssignmentSupplementItem}}, multiple access rules (or repeated save attempts on the same item within a single web request / form submit) trigger multiple calls to {{saveAllPurposeItemAccess()}}. If the internal cache/session isn't synced with the persistent unique index, it generates duplicate row inserts in a single transaction.

h3. Steps to Resolve or Work Around

# *Pull the Latest Trunk / Sakai JIRA Fix*:
#* Check Sakai Jira (under the {{ASSIGN}} project) for recent commits targeting {{AssignmentSupplementItemServiceImpl}} or {{saveAllPurposeItemAccess}}.
#* Look for Jira tickets addressing _All-Purpose Item Access duplication_ or {{uniqueAccessItem}} _constraint violations_.
# *Check the Logic in* {{AssignmentSupplementItemServiceImpl.java}}:
#* Inspect line {{393}} in {{AssignmentSupplementItemServiceImpl.saveAllPurposeItemAccess()}}.
#* Ensure that prior to calling {{saveOrUpdate()}}, existing access records for the specific {{itemId}} and user/role are either:
#** Queried and updated in place, or
#** Deleted before re-inserting new access entries for the supplement item.
# *Database Sanity Check*:
#* If testing on a local or development instance, inspect the database table for {{AssignmentAllPurposeItemAccess}} (or the underlying table holding the {{uniqueAccessItem}} constraint) to clean up stale duplicate rows if orphaned records exist.
